scenes.speaker: mentor_owl
lines: Every crate in this village wears a label, and every label can be peeled off and stuck on another crate.
That is all a variable is. The name is the label. The crate is the value.
So when someone tells you count = count + 1, they are not claiming a thing equals itself plus one.
They are saying: look in the crate, add one, and move the label to what you got.

scenes.prompt: a = 3, then b = a, then a = 10. What is b now?

options.text: An error — a was already used

scenes.reveal: b is 3. The line b = a happened once and copied what a held at that moment. Rebinding a afterwards moves only a's label.

scenes.prompt: Which line asks Python whether two things are the same, rather than telling it to bind a name?
scenes.reveal: == asks. = tells. Python refuses to run a file containing if x = 5, which is a kindness — the question was never asked.

scenes.speaker: mentor_owl
lines: Two doors, both carved with a plus sign. They do not do the same thing.
Give the left door two numbers and it adds them. Give the right door two pieces of text and it joins them.
The doors decide by looking at what you are carrying, not at what you meant.
Carry one of each, and neither door will open for you.

scenes.reveal: A TypeError. Python will not decide for you whether plus means arithmetic or joining, so it stops and says so. int("5") + 5 is 10; "5" + str(5) is "55". You choose.

scenes.prompt: The user types 7 at age = input("Age? "). What is in age?

options.text: The integer 7, because they typed digits

scenes.reveal: The string "7". input always hands back text, whatever was typed. age + 1 fails here; int(age) + 1 does not.

scenes.speaker: mentor_owl
lines: This lantern shows you what is in the room. It does not hand you anything.
print is that lantern. It puts a value where a person can see it.
Ask it for the value back and it gives you None, every time, without complaint.
Seeing a thing and holding a thing are different. Most of week six comes down to this.

scenes.prompt: After result = print("hello"), what is in result?
scenes.reveal: None. The word hello appeared on the screen as a side effect, and print handed back None. That is why a function which prints its answer has no answer anyone else can use.

scenes.speaker: mentor_owl
lines: Three crystals on the shelf, left to right. The shelf remembers the order; that is part of what it is.
But the surveyor who catalogued this room started at zero, standing in the doorway.
So the first crystal is number zero, and the third is number two.
There is no crystal number three, and the room will tell you so loudly.

scenes.prompt: scores = [90, 85, 100]. What does scores[3] give you?
scenes.reveal: An IndexError. Valid indexes are 0, 1 and 2 — the last is always one less than the length. scores[2] is 100, and scores[-1] is the same thing counted from the end.

scenes.instruction: Step the loop through [90, 85, 100] one item at a time and watch what the loop variable is bound to on each pass.
scenes.success_condition: The learner steps through all three items and sees the name rebound to the value, not to the position.

scenes.prompt: How many times does the block inside for i in range(3): run, and what is i on the last pass?

options.text: Three times; i is 2 at the end
Three times; i is 3 at the end

scenes.reveal: Three times, ending at 2. range stops before the number you give it — the same convention as indexing, which is exactly why range(len(scores)) walks a list's valid indexes.
